meta.provenance: terra-original; rules restated from primary law (law.cornell.edu, ecfr.gov, irs.gov); no commercial textbook text

cards.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
cards.title: IRS practice rights and representation forms
rule_lines: Unlimited practice: attorney + CPA + enrolled agent, none suspended or disbarred (31 CFR §10.3(a)-(c))
Enrolled actuary → listed pension-plan issues only; enrolled retirement plan agent → listed plan programs only
Form 2848 → authority to represent; Form 8821 → inspect and receive tax information only
Unenrolled preparer with AFSP Record of Completion → represent only at examination of returns the preparer signed
§10.7(c) no-enrollment cases: self, immediate family, employer full-time employee, partnership general partner, corporate officer
PTIN holder without credential or Record of Completion → prepare returns only; no representation
steps: Credential check: attorney / CPA / enrolled agent → unlimited practice
Actuary or retirement plan agent → confirm the issue is on the listed subjects
Preparer only → Record of Completion + signed the return + examination level only
No credential → test §10.7(c) list (self, family, employer, partnership, officer)
No match → prepare and sign only; representation refused
traps: Form 8821 treated as authority to represent; only Form 2848 (power of attorney) authorizes representation
Any PTIN holder or unrelated friend assumed able to appear at examination; no credential + no Record of Completion → no representation

example.q: Kim, a paid preparer with a PTIN but no credential and no AFSP Record of Completion, prepared and signed a client's 2025 return. IRS selects it for examination. May Kim represent the client, and which form applies if the client only wants Kim to receive IRS notices?
example.a: No representation. Only an attorney, CPA or enrolled agent (or a Record of Completion holder, limited) may represent. Receipt of information only → Form 8821.
work: Record of Completion? none → no limited rights

cites.label: IRS Pub. 947 Practice before the IRS and power of attorney

cards.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
cards.title: Circular 230 duties, fees and conflicts
rule_lines: §10.20 → submit properly requested IRS records promptly unless good-faith privilege applies
§10.21 → advise client of error or omission + consequences; duty runs to client, not IRS
§10.22 + §10.34 → due diligence; sign a position only with substantial authority, or reasonable basis + disclosure
§10.27 → contingent fee barred except: original-return exam, amended return within 120 days, interest/penalty refund, court case
§10.29 conflict: directly adverse clients need reasonable belief + informed consent confirmed in writing within 30 days
Written consents kept 36 months after the representation ends
steps: Client error found → advise client promptly of error + consequences
IRS asks for records → produce promptly unless good-faith privilege
Fee proposal → contingent? test against four permitted cases
Two clients → directly adverse? consent from every affected client, in writing
Return position → substantial authority, or reasonable basis + disclosure
traps: Client error reported to the IRS by the practitioner; §10.21 requires advising the client only
Contingent fee accepted for preparing an original return or for advice before filing; not one of the four permitted cases

example.q: A CPA agrees to prepare an original 2025 return for a fee equal to 10% of the refund. Is the fee arrangement permitted under Circular 230?
example.a: Not permitted. A contingent fee is barred for original-return preparation; allowed only for exam or challenge of a return, amended return within 120 days of exam notice, interest/penalty refund, or court case.
work: Fee depends on refund → contingent fee
Original return preparation → not an exam, challenge or court case

cards.topic: Internal Revenue Code and regulations related to tax return preparers
cards.title: Preparer penalties and preparer rules
rule_lines: Preparer = paid to prepare all or a substantial part of a return; signing not required (IRC §7701(a)(36))
Unreasonable position → greater of $1,000 or 50% of income derived (IRC §6694(a))
Willful or reckless understatement → greater of $5,000 or 75% of income derived (IRC §6694(b))
Position safe: substantial authority, or reasonable basis + disclosure; reportable transaction needs more-likely-than-not belief
Due diligence penalty (IRC §6695(g)): EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, head of household; applies even if credit is correct
Return copy due when presented for signature (§6695(a)); disclosure or use needs consent except to another U.S. preparer (§7216)
steps: Identify preparer: compensation + all or substantial part of the return
Test the position: substantial authority? reasonable basis + disclosure? reportable transaction?
Fails test → unreasonable (50% regime); willful or reckless → 75% regime
Penalty = MAX(fixed floor, rate × income derived from the return)
traps: Floor amount used alone; the percentage of income derived can be larger, so take the greater
Rates mixed: 50% goes with unreasonable position, 75% with willful or reckless conduct

example.q: A preparer is paid $3,000 for a return that contains an unreasonable undisclosed position. What is the §6694(a) penalty? What if the conduct was willful?
example.a: Unreasonable position: $1,500. Willful or reckless: $5,000.

cites.label: IRC §6694 Understatement of taxpayer's liability by tax return preparer

cards.topic: AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services and Code of Professional Conduct
cards.title: AICPA tax standards and confidentiality
rule_lines: Prior-year client error → advise client + recommend correction; no duty to notify the IRS
Client information needs consent; exceptions include valid enforceable subpoena or summons and peer review
Reasonable client estimates allowed when exact data impractical; not presented as exact
Return answer left blank only for unavailable information, reasonable uncertainty or immateriality; not for audit risk
Prior returns usable; inquire when client information looks incorrect, incomplete or inconsistent
No duty to update advice for later law changes unless agreed or assisting implementation
steps: Error found → tell client + explain consequences + recommend correction
Third-party request → consent, or exception (subpoena, peer review)
Missing data → reasonable estimate, labeled as an estimate
Advice already given → update only if engagement requires it
traps: Member notifies the IRS of a prior-year error; disclosure needs client consent unless a legal exception applies
Member assumed to owe ongoing advice updates after law changes; the duty exists only by agreement or implementation

example.q: A member prepared a client's 2024 return and, while preparing 2025, finds 2024 income was omitted. What must the member do?
example.a: Advise the client promptly of the error and its consequences and recommend correction. No duty to inform the IRS; disclosure without consent is barred.
work: IRS notice by member → confidential information, needs consent
Client refuses correction → member may consider withdrawal

cites.label: AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services

cards.title: Circular 230 discipline and sanctions
rule_lines: OPR administers Circular 230; sanctions: censure, suspension, disbarment, monetary penalty (§10.50)
Censure = public reprimand; right to practice continues
Monetary penalty ≤ gross income derived from the sanctionable conduct (§10.50(c))
Disreputable conduct (§10.51): false information, willful failure to file own return; unsuccessful competent position is not
Expedited suspension (§10.82): within 5 years, license lost for cause, or conviction of tax crime or dishonesty crime
ALJ decision → appeal to Secretary of the Treasury; disbarred practitioner may seek reinstatement after 5 years
steps: Conduct → §10.51 disreputable? (fraud, false information, willful non-filing)
Sanction ladder → censure < suspension < disbarment; monetary penalty capped
Conviction or license loss → expedited suspension route
Decision → ALJ initial decision → Secretary of the Treasury appeal
traps: Penalty measured as 50% or 75% of fee (preparer-penalty measure); Circular 230 cap is gross income derived
Tax Court or IRS Appeals assumed to hear discipline appeals; ALJ decisions go to the Secretary of the Treasury

example.q: A practitioner earned $8,000 from conduct found sanctionable under Circular 230. What is the maximum monetary penalty, and where is the ALJ decision appealed?
example.a: Maximum $8,000. Appeal goes to the Secretary of the Treasury.
work: Cap = gross income derived from the conduct = $8,000
ALJ decision → Secretary of the Treasury (not Tax Court)

cards.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
cards.title: Assessment and refund time limits
rule_lines: Assessment period: 3 years from filing; early return treated as filed on due date (IRC §6501(a),(b)(1))
Omission of more than 25% of gross income stated on the return → 6 years (§6501(e)(1)(A))
False or fraudulent return, willful evasion, or no return → no limit (§6501(c))
Period extended by written agreement made before expiry (§6501(c)(4))
Refund claim: later of 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment (§6511(a))
Refund amount ≤ tax paid in look-back: 3 years + extension, or 2 years (§6511(b)(2))
steps: Find deemed filing date → later of actual filing and due date
Add 3 years; omission > 25% of stated gross income → add 6
Fraud or nonfiler → no expiry
Refund → filing date + 3 years, or payment date + 2 years
traps: Early filing date used as the clock start; the return is treated as filed on the due date
Amended return or >25% omission read as unlimited; omission gives 6 years, only fraud or no return is unlimited

example.q: A calendar-year individual filed the 2025 return on March 1, 2026 (due April 15, 2026), showing gross income of $100,000. IRS later finds $30,000 of omitted income (no fraud). By what date must IRS assess?

cites.label: IRC §6501 Limitations on assessment and collection
IRC §6511 Limitations on credit or refund

cards.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
cards.title: Examination, appeals and courts
rule_lines: Notice of deficiency → 90 days to petition Tax Court (150 if outside U.S.); assessment barred meanwhile (IRC §6213(a))
Tax Court: no prepayment; district court or Court of Federal Claims: pay the tax, then sue for refund
Small tax case (§7463): disputed amount ≤ $50,000 per year; decision not appealable
Appeals: Tax Court → circuit of taxpayer residence (§7482(b)); Court of Federal Claims → Federal Circuit
Summons (§7602) not self-enforcing; IRS petitions district court (§7604); third-party summons: 20 days to begin quash proceeding (§7609(b)(2))
Interview audio recording: taxpayer gives 10 days advance notice, in writing (§7521(a); Pub. 556)
steps: Examination → 30-day letter → Appeals protest
No agreement → notice of deficiency → count 90 days
Choose forum → Tax Court (no prepayment) vs pay-and-sue
Appeal → circuit by residence (Tax Court), Federal Circuit (Court of Federal Claims)
traps: Time limits mixed up: 30 days is the 30-day letter, 120 days is not a period here, 150 days needs an address outside the U.S.
Summons treated as self-enforcing, or enforceable by the Tax Court; only a district court enforces

example.q: A notice of deficiency addressed to a U.S. resident is mailed March 2, 2026. What is the last day to petition the Tax Court?
work: May 31, 2026 is a Sunday → next business day (IRC §7503)

cites.label: IRC §7609 Special procedures for third-party summonses
IRS Pub. 556 Examination of returns (10-day recording notice)

cards.title: Substantiation, records and disclosure
rule_lines: Travel, gifts, listed property need strict proof: amount + time + place + business purpose (IRC §274(d))
Receipt needed for lodging and any other expense of $75 or more (Reg. §1.274-5(c)(2)(iii))
Ordinary expenses need reasonable records only (IRC §6001)
Substantial understatement reduced by substantial authority, or adequate disclosure + reasonable basis (§6662(d)(2)(B))
Disclosure on Form 8275; position contrary to a regulation → Form 8275-R; disclosure gives no relief for tax shelters
FBAR (FinCEN 114): aggregate foreign accounts over $10,000 at any time; due April 15, automatic extension to October 15
steps: Expense type → strict category (travel, gifts, listed property) or ordinary
Under $75 non-lodging → log with amount, time, place, purpose
Position weak → substantial authority? else reasonable basis + Form 8275 / 8275-R
Foreign accounts → sum maximum values → over $10,000 → FBAR
traps: Receipt required for every expense; under $75 (other than lodging) a log with the four elements is enough
Disclosure assumed to cure any weak position; no relief for tax shelters, and a position without reasonable basis is not cured

example.q: A taxpayer holds foreign accounts with maximum values of $6,000 (April) and $5,000 (October), each at a different bank. Is an FBAR required? On a business trip, which item needs a receipt: $60 taxi or $60 hotel?
example.a: FBAR required: aggregate $11,000 exceeds $10,000. Hotel needs a receipt; taxi under $75 needs only a log.
work: Lodging always needs a receipt; other expenses under $75 → log entry

cites.label: IRS: Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)

cards.title: Civil penalties and reasonable cause
rule_lines: Failure to file: 5% per month up to 25%, reduced by failure-to-pay for overlapping months (IRC §6651(a)(1),(c)(1))
Failure to pay: 0.5% per month up to 25%; overlapping months 4.5% + 0.5% = 5% (§6651(a)(2))
Accuracy-related: 20% of underpayment for negligence, substantial understatement, substantial valuation misstatement (§6662)
Gross valuation misstatement (basis 200% or more of correct) → 40% (§6662(h))
Civil fraud → 75%, proved by clear and convincing evidence (§6663)
Reasonable cause + good faith defeats §6662; reliance on an agent to file on time does not (Boyle)
steps: Late return + unpaid tax → months late (part of a month counts)
Combined rate = 5% per overlapping month, capped at 25% for failure to file
Understatement → identify one accuracy ground → 20% (or 40%); no stacking
Fraud proven → 75% replaces accuracy penalty on that portion
traps: Full 5% failure-to-file added to 0.5% failure-to-pay; overlapping months use 4.5% + 0.5%
Rates stacked (20% + 20%, or 20% + 75%) for one underpayment; only one accuracy-related penalty per portion

example.q: A taxpayer files 3 months and 10 days after the due date (4 months or part of a month) with $10,000 of tax unpaid throughout. Compute failure-to-file plus failure-to-pay penalties, ignoring interest.

cites.label: IRC §6651 Failure to file or pay tax
IRC §7454 Burden of proof in fraud cases

cards.title: Tax authority hierarchy
rule_lines: Order: Code (statute) → Treasury regulations → revenue rulings and procedures → court decisions and private rulings
Regulations interpret the Code and rank below it (IRC §7805(a))
Private letter ruling binds only the taxpayer who received it; not precedent for others (IRC §6110(k)(3))
Substantial authority includes statutes, regulations, rulings, notices, court cases; excludes treatises and legal periodicals (Reg. §1.6662-4(d)(3))
Position contrary to a regulation → disclose on Form 8275-R
steps: Statute on point → applies, no lower source overrides
Regulation → controls over ruling; ruling → IRS position only
Private ruling → own taxpayer only; other sources supply support, not precedent
traps: Revenue ruling or regulation placed above the Code; the Code outranks all of them
Private letter ruling cited as precedent; only its recipient may rely on it

example.q: A regulation and a private letter ruling issued to another taxpayer conflict on a question. Which controls, and can a third taxpayer rely on the private ruling?
example.a: The regulation controls; a third taxpayer may not rely on the private ruling as precedent.

cites.label: IRC §6110 Public inspection of written determinations

cards.title: Privilege, liability and criminal limits
rule_lines: Tax practitioner privilege (IRC §7525): tax advice, federally authorized practitioner, noncriminal federal tax matters only
Not covered: criminal cases, state matters, SEC proceedings, tax shelter promotion, return preparation information
Couch: no Fifth Amendment shield for records held by an accountant; no federal accountant-client privilege
Kovel: accountant hired by attorney to help give legal advice → attorney-client privilege
Negligence to client = failure of ordinary care; third parties (Ultramares): privity, or fraud / constructive fraud
Criminal limitations: 6 years for evasion and false returns, 3 years general (IRC §6531)
steps: Communication type → tax advice? or return preparation data?
Forum → noncriminal federal tax proceeding? else §7525 unavailable
Waiver check → voluntary disclosure to outsider waives; IRS request does not
Liability → client (negligence, contract, fraud) vs third party (privity rule)
traps: §7525 privilege applied in criminal or state proceedings; it reaches only noncriminal federal tax matters
Taxpayer records held by the accountant assumed protected by the Fifth Amendment; Couch says no

example.q: The IRS summons a CPA's workpapers used to prepare a client's 2024 return; the client invokes the Fifth Amendment and §7525. Is the CPA protected?
example.a: No. Fifth Amendment does not protect records in the accountant's hands (Couch), and §7525 does not cover return-preparation information.
work: Fifth Amendment → personal to the taxpayer; not compelled testimony from the client
§7525 → tax advice only; preparation data excluded

cards.topic: Agency: authority of agents and principals
cards.title: Agent authority
rule_lines: Actual authority: express (stated) or implied (reasonably necessary to carry out the express grant)
Apparent authority: principal's manifestation to the third party + third party's reasonable belief
Agent's own statements alone never create apparent authority
Ending actual authority does not end apparent authority until the third party is told
Partner binds the partnership for acts apparently in the ordinary course; outside it, all other partners must authorize
Person consenting to be represented as a partner is liable to a relying third party
steps: Grant words → express; needed acts → implied
Third-party facts → principal's manifestation? reasonable reliance?
Agent fired → actual ends; notify prior dealers to end apparent
Partner act → ordinary course? else all-partner authorization
traps: Apparent authority read as arising from the agent's own claims; it comes from the principal's conduct
Firing the agent assumed to end all authority; apparent authority continues toward third parties not notified

example.q: An owner tells the office manager, "You are in charge of keeping the office running." Without asking again, the manager hires a cleaning service. Which authority supports the hiring?
example.a: Implied actual authority, since cleaning is reasonably necessary to the express duty.
work: Cleaning is needed to keep an office running → implied actual authority
Not express: cleaning was never mentioned

cites.label: Cornell Wex: Agency (overview; primary source is common law or uniform act, not on approved hosts)
Cornell Wex: Apparent authority (overview; primary source is common law or uniform act, not on approved hosts)

cards.topic: Agency: duties and liabilities of agents and principals
cards.title: Agent and principal duties and liability
rule_lines: Agent duties: loyalty (no secret benefit), obedience, care; principal duties: compensation, indemnity for authorized acts
Principal liable for employee torts within scope of employment (respondeat superior)
Disclosed principal: principal bound, agent not; undisclosed principal: agent is a party, principal also bound
Ratification: knowing acceptance of benefits affirms the whole transaction
Agent's knowledge gained within scope is imputed to the principal
Signature clearly in representative form for a named principal → representative not liable on the instrument (UCC §3-402)
steps: Duty breach → loyalty, obedience or care?
Tort → scope of employment? then principal liable too
Contract → principal disclosed, partially disclosed, undisclosed
Unauthorized act → ratification only by full-knowledge acceptance
traps: Employer assumed not liable for an employee's negligence on a delivery route; within scope, it is liable
Ratification limited to the favorable part; a principal cannot keep the benefit and disown the rest

example.q: An agent, acting for an undisclosed principal, signs a supply contract in the agent's own name. Who is liable?
example.a: The agent is a party and liable; the principal is also bound once identified.
work: Undisclosed principal → agent treated as party

cites.label: Cornell Wex: Respondeat superior (overview; primary source is common law or uniform act, not on approved hosts)
Cornell Wex: Agency (overview; primary source is common law or uniform act, not on approved hosts)

cards.title: Contract formation and sales of goods rules
rule_lines: Contract = mutual assent + consideration + capacity + legal purpose; bare gift promise lacks consideration
Firm offer (UCC §2-205): merchant, signed writing, irrevocable up to 3 months without consideration
Statute of frauds for goods: signed writing if price $500 or more (UCC §2-201), with exceptions
Modification of a goods contract needs no consideration, only good faith (UCC §2-209)
Mailbox rule: acceptance effective on dispatch; revocation effective on receipt
Added terms in acceptance: contract forms; between merchants they are proposals, excluded if offer limits acceptance (§2-207)
steps: Offer → definite terms communicated
Acceptance → mirror image (common law) or definite expression (UCC)
Consideration → bargained-for exchange, except UCC modification and firm offer
Goods $500 or more → writing or exception
traps: Common-law consideration rule applied to a merchant's firm offer or a UCC modification
Acceptance treated as effective on receipt; under the mailbox rule it is effective on dispatch

example.q: A merchant signs a writing promising to hold an offer to sell goods open for 30 days. On day 10 she revokes. Is the offer still open?
example.a: Yes. A merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable up to 3 months without consideration.

cards.title: Performance, risk of loss and discharge
rule_lines: Perfect tender: buyer may reject goods that fail to conform (UCC §2-601); seller may cure within contract time (§2-508)
Substantial performance: recovery = contract price − cost of deficiency
Reasonable insecurity → demand adequate assurance in writing; failure within reasonable time = repudiation (§2-609)
Shipment contract: risk of loss passes to buyer on delivery to carrier (§2-509(1)(a))
Impracticability excuses seller if basic assumption fails; seller allocates supply fairly and notifies (§2-615)
Novation substitutes a party and releases the original obligor
steps: Tender conforms? no → reject, accept, or partial
Time left → seller notice of cure + conforming delivery
Risk of loss → shipment vs destination contract
Discharge route → performance, agreement, novation, impracticability
traps: Substantial performance recovery computed as the deficiency alone; recovery is price less deficiency
Risk of loss placed on the seller until the buyer receives shipment goods; carrier delivery shifts risk in a shipment contract

example.q: A builder substantially performs an $80,000 contract; the deficiency cost is $3,000. What can the builder recover?
work: Substantial performance → builder may enforce the contract

cites.label: UCC §2-601 Buyer's rights on improper delivery
UCC §2-615 Excuse by failure of presupposed conditions

cards.title: Breach remedies, warranties and limitations
rule_lines: Buyer cover: (cover price − contract price) × quantity + incidental damages (UCC §2-712)
Seller's damages: contract price − market price + incidental damages (§2-708(1)); action for price for identified goods not resalable (§2-709)
Specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances (§2-716)
Statute of limitations for sales: 4 years from accrual, parties may reduce to 1 year, not extend (§2-725)
Implied warranty of merchantability from a merchant; disclaimer must mention merchantability and be conspicuous (§2-314, §2-316)
Limited remedy failing its essential purpose → UCC remedies available (§2-719(2))
steps: Breach by seller → cover, market damages, or specific performance
Breach by buyer → resale or market damages, or price action
Add incidental damages; subtract expenses saved
Check warranty, disclaimer, limitation of remedy, time limit
traps: Cover damages computed as the full cost of substitute goods; only the excess over the contract price counts
Six-year general contract period applied; sales of goods use a 4-year period from accrual

example.q: A buyer covers by purchasing 5,000 units at $3.40; the contract price was $3.00. Incidental damages are $150. What are cover damages?

cards.title: Secured transactions and suretyship
rule_lines: Attachment: value + debtor rights in collateral + authenticated security agreement describing collateral (or possession) (UCC §9-203)
Perfection: filing a financing statement; possession for goods; automatic for consumer-goods purchase-money interest (§9-310, §9-313)
Purchase-money interest perfected within 20 days after debtor takes possession has priority over earlier filer (§9-324(a))
Continuation statement effective only within 6 months before the 5-year lapse (§9-515)
Sale proceeds: reasonable expenses first, then debt; debtor owes deficiency (§9-608, §9-615)
Guarantor who pays: reimbursement from principal debtor + subrogation; creditor extension discharges to extent of loss
steps: Attach → value, rights, agreement or possession
Perfect → file, possess, or automatic
Priority → first to file or perfect; PMSI within 20 days
Default → dispose collateral → expenses → debt → deficiency
traps: Attachment assumed with only value and rights in collateral; a security agreement (or possession) is also required
Sale proceeds applied to debt before expenses; expenses are paid first

example.q: Collateral sells for $38,000; reasonable sale expenses are $3,000; the debt is $60,000. What is the deficiency?

cites.label: UCC §9-310 When filing is required to perfect
UCC §9-324 Priority of purchase-money security interests
UCC §9-515 Duration and effectiveness of financing statement
UCC §9-615 Application of proceeds of disposition

cards.title: Employer mandate and premium tax credit
rule_lines: Applicable large employer: full-time employees + part-time hours ÷ 120 ≥ 50 (IRC §4980H(c)(2))
Full-time employee: average at least 30 hours per week or 130 hours per month
§4980H(a): under 95% offered + one credit recipient → payment = amount × (full-time employees − 30)
§4980H(b): lesser of amount × credit recipients or the (a) amount cap
Seasonal exception: workforce over 50 for 120 days or fewer, excess seasonal
Premium credit denied for months with affordable minimum-value employer coverage; repayment cap ends after 2025 [OBBBA]
steps: Count FTEs → full-time + part-time hours ÷ 120
≥ 50 → applicable large employer
95% offer test → (a) or (b) payment
Payment amounts are given in the question
traps: Part-time hours divided by 40 instead of 120 when counting equivalents
Employer payment computed on credit recipients only under (a); it uses all full-time employees less 30

example.q: An employer has 35 full-time employees and part-time employees who worked 3,600 hours in total in a month. Is it an applicable large employer?
example.a: Yes. 65 full-time equivalents is at least 50.

cards.title: Employee or independent contractor
rule_lines: Common-law test: right to control how and by what means the work is done (Reg. §31.3121(d)-1(c))
Evidence groups: behavioral control, financial control, relationship of parties
Labels and forms filed do not control; the substance of control does
Statutory employees for FICA: agent-driver, full-time life insurance salesperson, home worker, traveling salesperson (IRC §3121(d)(3))
Uncertain status → Form SS-8 determination request
steps: Right to direct details → employee
Firm supplies tools and bears profit or loss → contractor factors
Check statutory employee list
traps: Contract label 'independent contractor' treated as controlling; substance of control decides
Full-time insurance salesperson assumed contractor because of no common-law control; the statute makes the person an employee

example.q: A full-time life insurance salesperson works for one insurer under a contract calling her an independent contractor. FICA status?
example.a: Statutory employee for FICA.
work: Full-time life insurance salesperson is a listed category (§3121(d)(3)(B))

cards.title: Bankruptcy chapters, stay, discharge and avoidance
rule_lines: Chapter 7: trustee liquidation; Chapter 11: reorganization; Chapter 13: individual repayment plan with regular income
Automatic stay on filing halts civil collection; it does not stay criminal proceedings (11 U.S.C. §362)
Chapter 7 discharge barred if prior chapter 7 discharge in case commenced within 8 years (§727(a)(8))
Nondischargeable: debts obtained by fraud or false pretenses, recent taxes, support, most student loans (§523)
Preference (§547): transfer to creditor on antecedent debt within 90 days (1 year for insiders) while insolvent
Fraudulent transfer: less than reasonably equivalent value within 2 years and insolvent (§548)
steps: Chapter → liquidate (7), reorganize (11), individual plan (13)
Petition → automatic stay, except criminal and support items
Trustee avoidance → preference 90 days / fraudulent 2 years
Distribution → administrative and priority claims first, then general claims pro rata
traps: Chapter 13 described as corporate liquidation; it is an individual repayment plan
Preference reach-back set at 1 year for all creditors; 90 days applies to non-insiders

example.q: An estate has $60,000. Administrative and priority tax claims total $30,000; timely general unsecured claims total $100,000. What does a $20,000 general claim receive?

cards.title: Foreign Corrupt Practices Act
rule_lines: Anti-bribery: corrupt offer or payment to a foreign official to obtain or retain business (15 U.S.C. §78dd-1, -2)
Covers issuers, domestic concerns, and payments through intermediaries with knowledge
Exception: facilitating payment for routine governmental action; must be accurately recorded
Affirmative defenses: payment lawful under written local law; reasonable bona fide promotional or contract expenditure
Accounting provisions for issuers: accurate books and records in reasonable detail (§78m(b)(2)(A))
Internal accounting controls duty applies independently of any bribe (§78m(b)(2)(B))
steps: Payer → issuer or domestic concern?
Recipient → foreign official? purpose → obtain or retain business?
Exception or defense → routine action, local law, bona fide expenditure
Books → accurately recorded?
traps: Payment through an agent treated as outside the statute; knowledge that it reaches an official makes it covered
Accounting provisions assumed to apply only if a bribe occurred; internal controls duty stands alone

example.q: A U.S. issuer pays $200 to a foreign clerk to speed processing of a routine permit and records it accurately. Anti-bribery and accounting violation?
example.a: No violation under the routine governmental action exception; accurate recording avoids an accounting violation.
work: Routine governmental action → facilitating payment exception
Local law may still prohibit it

cites.label: 15 U.S.C. §78dd-1 Prohibited foreign trade practices by issuers
15 U.S.C. §78m Periodical and other reports (accounting provisions)

cards.title: FICA, FUTA and payroll penalties
rule_lines: FICA: employee 6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare, employer matches; employee share cannot be waived (IRC §3101, §3111)
Additional Medicare tax 0.9% withheld on wages over $200,000 regardless of filing status
FUTA: employer only; 6.0% on first $7,000 per employee, 5.4% credit for timely state tax → net 0.6% (§3301, §3302)
Deposit penalty: 2% (1-5 days late), 5% (6-15 days), 10% (over 15 days) (§6656)
Trust fund recovery penalty: responsible person who willfully fails to pay over withheld tax (§6672)
Income tax withholding follows Form W-4; quarterly Form 941, annual Form 940
steps: Wages → FICA at 7.65% each side up to wage base
FUTA wage base $7,000 × employees × net rate
Late deposit → days late → penalty tier × deposit
traps: Net FUTA rate applied to all wages; it applies only to the first $7,000 per employee
Employee waiver accepted for FICA; the employer must withhold both parts

example.q: An employer has 10 employees each paid over $7,000; timely state unemployment tax was paid. What is federal FUTA?

cards.title: Cost basis and lump-sum allocation
rule_lines: Cost basis = cash paid + liabilities assumed + capitalized acquisition costs (IRC §1012)
Capitalize: sales tax, freight, installation, title search, recording, legal fees to acquire title
Not basis: loan costs (amortized over loan term), insurance, interest, post-installation training
Lump-sum purchase → allocate total cost by relative fair market value (land vs building)
Purchase-money debt is basis from day one; interest on it is expense, not basis
Land is not depreciable; only the building share is recovered
steps: List cost items → price + debt assumed + capitalizable closing costs
Remove non-basis items (loan fees, insurance, interest)
Allocate total: FMV share × total cost
Land share stays; building share enters depreciation
traps: Loan origination fees added to basis; they are amortized over the loan term
Cost allocated by book value or 50/50; the split follows relative fair market value

cards.title: Adjusted, gift, inherited and converted basis
rule_lines: Adjusted basis = cost + improvements − depreciation allowed or allowable, whichever is greater (IRC §1016)
Gift: donee takes donor basis; if FMV at gift is lower, that FMV is the basis for a loss (§1015(a))
Gift tax paid on net appreciation increases donee basis (§1015(d))
Inherited: basis = FMV at date of death (or alternate valuation date); holding period long-term (§1014, §1223(9))
Personal → business conversion: basis for depreciation and loss = lesser of adjusted basis or FMV (Reg. §1.168(i)-4(b))
Spouse transfer or divorce transfer: carryover basis, no gain or loss (§1041)
steps: Start → cost or acquisition basis
Add improvements; subtract depreciation allowed or allowable
Gift → compare sale price with donor basis and FMV at gift
Sale price between donor basis and gift-date FMV → no gain, no loss
traps: Gain and loss both measured from donor basis; when FMV at gift is lower, loss uses that FMV
Depreciation reduces basis only when claimed; allowed or allowable reduces basis even if unclaimed

example.q: Donor basis $40,000, FMV at gift $30,000. The donee later sells for $50,000, or alternatively for $25,000. Recognized amount in each case?
work: Sale $50,000 > donor basis $40,000 → gain basis $40,000 → gain $10,000
Sale between $30,000 and $40,000 → no gain, no loss

cards.title: MACRS classes and conventions
rule_lines: 5-year: computers, cars, light trucks; 7-year: furniture, most equipment (IRC §168(e)(3))
Residential rental 27.5-year straight-line; nonresidential real property 39-year straight-line; mid-month convention

steps: Classify property → recovery period and method
Test Q4 basis ÷ total personal property basis > 40% → mid-quarter, else half-year
Pick table rate by class + convention + year
Depreciation = depreciable basis × table rate
traps: Real property included in the 40% test; only personal property counts
Land included in the 39-year or 27.5-year base; land is never depreciable

Bonus depreciation (§168(k)): 100% for property acquired after Jan. 19, 2025 [OBBBA; tested from 2026-07-01]
Order: §179 first → bonus on the rest → regular MACRS on remaining basis

§197 intangibles: 15-year straight-line from month acquired; start-up and organizational costs: $5,000 first-year deduction, phased out over $50,000

Reduce basis by §179 → apply bonus (if not elected out) → MACRS on remainder
Listed property → business-use % > 50%? else straight-line, no §179
Intangible → 15-year straight-line; start-up cost → $5,000 less excess over $50,000

Listed property at 50% or less business use assumed eligible; business use must exceed 50%

Excluded: gifts and inheritances, life insurance proceeds, state and local bond interest (IRC §102, §101, §103)

Test each exclusion: source, purpose, dollar cap
Cap exceeded → excess is wages or other income
Total includible = taxable items + excess over caps
traps: Unemployment compensation treated as excluded; it is fully taxable
Whole educational assistance excluded; only $5,250 per year is excluded, the excess is wages

rule_lines: Social Security taxable up to 85%; provisional income = other AGI + tax-exempt interest + 50% of benefits (IRC §86)
Base amounts: single $25,000 and $34,000; married filing jointly $32,000 and $44,000
Tier 1: up to 50% of benefits; tier 2: 85% above upper base; total capped at 85% of benefits
Annuity: exclusion ratio = investment ÷ expected return; exclusion stops once investment is recovered (IRC §72)
Home sale exclusion: $250,000 single, $500,000 joint; owned and used 2 of last 5 years (IRC §121)
Qualified dividends and long-term gains use capital gain rates; state bond interest excluded
steps: Provisional income = AGI (without benefits) + tax-exempt interest + 50% of benefits
Below lower base → 0; between bases → up to 50%; above upper base → add 85% of excess
Cap total at 85% × benefits

Tax-exempt interest left out of provisional income, or benefits counted at 100% instead of 50%

rule_lines: Partnership and S corporation income passes to owners; separately stated items keep their character (IRC §702(a), §1366(a))
Separately stated: capital gains, §179, charitable contributions, interest, other items that affect owners differently
Partner taxed on distributive share + guaranteed payments whether or not cash is distributed
Cash distributions reduce basis; taxed only when above basis
Loss limits in order: basis → at-risk → passive activity → excess business loss

Add guaranteed payments as ordinary income
Basis → + income, − distributions and losses
Apply loss limits in order

Ordinary operating expenses separately stated; only items that affect owners differently are separately stated

steps: Add itemized categories → apply floors and caps
SALT = lesser of taxes paid or cap after phase-down

rule_lines: Standard deduction 2026: $16,100 single or MFS, $24,150 HOH, $32,200 joint; add $1,650 age 65+ or blind ($2,050 unmarried)
Dependent standard deduction: greater of $1,350 or earned income + $450, not above the basic amount

cards.title: Capital losses, wash sales and other loss rules
rule_lines: Net capital loss deduction ≤ $3,000 ($1,500 MFS); excess carries forward indefinitely, keeping character (IRC §1211(b), §1212(b))
Wash sale: identical stock bought within 30 days before or after sale; loss added to new basis (§1091)
Personal-use property losses not deductible; investment property losses are (IRC §165(c))
Loss on sale to a related party disallowed; worthless securities treated as sold on last day of year (§267, §165(g))
§1244 stock: ordinary loss up to $50,000 ($100,000 joint) per year
NOL carried forward indefinitely; deduction ≤ 80% of taxable income (IRC §172)
steps: Net short-term and long-term separately → combine net results
Net loss → deduct up to $3,000 against ordinary income
Remainder → carryforward, same short or long character
Wash sale → disallow loss, add to replacement basis

Loss on personal-use property (car, home, furniture) deducted; only investment or business property losses count

cards.title: Basis, at-risk, passive activity and excess business loss
rule_lines: Loss limit order: stock or outside basis → at-risk (§465) → passive activity (§469) → excess business loss (§461(l))
Passive losses offset passive income only; suspended losses released on full taxable disposition to an unrelated party
Rental allowance $25,000 with active participation; reduced 50% of MAGI over $100,000; gone at $150,000 (§469(i))
Real estate professional: over 750 hours and more than half of personal services in real property trades
Excess business loss 2026: above $256,000 ($512,000 joint) → NOL carryforward; limit permanent [OBBBA; tested from 2026-07-01]
Partner loss limited to outside basis; excess carried forward until basis restored (§704(d))
steps: Basis first → loss allowed up to basis
At-risk amount next → then passive activity test
Passive rental → $25,000 allowance less 50% × (MAGI − $100,000)
Aggregate business loss > threshold → excess becomes NOL

Passive loss used against wages or portfolio income; it offsets only passive income until disposition

rule_lines: Married at year end → joint or separate; year of spouse death → joint if survivor not remarried (IRC §7703)

Dependent? qualifying child tests (relationship, age, residency, support) or qualifying relative tests
Home costs paid > 50% + qualifying person → HOH

Head of household claimed while married and living together; considered unmarried needs spouse absent last 6 months

Recognized gain = lesser of realized gain or boot

cards.title: Corporate distributions and liquidation
rule_lines: Dividend to extent of current or accumulated E&P; current E&P counts despite an accumulated deficit (IRC §316)

cards.title: S corporation eligibility and election
rule_lines: Eligible corporation: domestic, up to 100 shareholders (family members count as one), one class of stock (IRC §1361)

Ineligible: insurance companies under subchapter L, certain financial institutions; accumulated E&P does not bar election
Form 2553 by 15th day of 3rd month of tax year to be effective that year; all shareholders consent

steps: Corporation test → domestic, eligible type, one class of stock
Shareholder test → count (family as one), type, consents
File Form 2553 → within 2 months + 15 days of year start
Later disqualifying event → termination on that date

Partnership or corporate shareholder accepted; only individuals, estates and certain trusts qualify

example.q: A new calendar-year corporation's tax year begins February 1, 2026. What is the last day to file Form 2553 for S status effective for 2026?

rule_lines: Stock basis + for income (ordinary, separately stated, tax-exempt), contributions
Basis − in order: distributions, nondeductible expenses, then losses (Reg. §1.1367-1(f))
Loss limited to stock basis then debt basis; excess suspended indefinitely (IRC §1366(d))

Corporate liabilities to outsiders do not add to basis, unlike partnerships
Repayment of debt with reduced basis → gain in proportion

− distributions → − nondeductible → − losses

cards.title: S corporation distributions and corporate-level taxes
rule_lines: No C-corporation E&P: distribution reduces stock basis; excess over basis is capital gain (IRC §1368(b))
With C E&P: AAA distributed first, then E&P as dividend, then basis, then gain (§1368(c))
Built-in gains tax: 21% on net recognized built-in gain during 5-year recognition period (§1374)
Excess passive income tax: 21% of excess net passive income when passive receipts exceed 25% and C E&P exists (§1375)
Distribution of appreciated property → gain recognized and passed through (§311(b))
Reasonable compensation to shareholder-employees; C corporation profits face second layer of tax on distribution
steps: Distribution → C E&P present? no → basis first
Yes → AAA, then E&P, then basis, then gain
Sale within recognition period → built-in gain limited to remaining NUBIG
Tax = 21% × recognized built-in gain
traps: Built-in gains tax applied to sales after the 5-year period or to post-conversion appreciation; neither is taxed
Excess passive income tax computed on all passive income; only excess net passive income is taxed

cards.title: Partnership ordinary income and separately stated items
rule_lines: Ordinary income deducts wages, rent, guaranteed payments, regular depreciation; separately stated items go to K-1 (IRC §702, §703)

Guaranteed payment for services: ordinary income to partner, deduction or capitalized cost to partnership (§707(c))
Form 1065 due March 15 (calendar year); automatic 6-month extension to September 15
Partner reports distributive share whether or not distributed
steps: Revenue − ordinary expenses (incl. guaranteed payments) = ordinary income
Pull out separately stated items
Allocate by partnership agreement → K-1
traps: Charitable contributions deducted in ordinary income; they are separately stated
Guaranteed payment ignored by the partnership; it is deducted there and ordinary income to the recipient

Basis − distributions (cash + property basis), losses, nondeductible expenses, decrease in share of liabilities (§752(b))

steps: Start: contributions + liability share
+ income and tax-exempt income
− distributions, then − losses and nondeductible expenses

rule_lines: Current distribution: gain only if cash exceeds outside basis; no partner loss (IRC §731(a)(1))
Distributed property takes partnership basis, limited to remaining outside basis (§732(a))
Liquidating distribution of only cash, receivables, inventory: loss = basis − cash − receivable and inventory basis (§731(a)(2))
Sale of interest: capital gain or loss, except unrealized receivables and inventory → ordinary (§741, §751)
Amount realized includes relief of partnership liabilities (§752(d))
§754 election → transferee basis adjustment = outside basis − share of inside basis (§743(b))

Property → lesser of inside basis or remaining outside basis
Sale → amount realized incl. liability relief − outside basis

Tax year: majority-interest year (over 50% of profits and capital), then principal partners (§706(b))
Capital interest for services taxable at value; profits interest generally not taxed on receipt (Rev. Proc. 93-27, 2001-43)
Precontribution gain recognized by contributor on later sale, not shared

Election? Form 8832 within 75-day look-back

rule_lines: §501(c)(3): organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes; no private inurement of net earnings

Remove excluded income
